BEGINNING OF PROCEEDINGS - TAPE 1

This is a humid morning. This is Friday, the eleventh of July 1980. This is the first tape that we're going to be doing in the Oral History Project with Maxine Sullivan. I thought with the first session what we do is play both of your recording sessions, and play them session by session, and get your comments on them -- see if that will trigger off some of your recollections and so on. And then, at the second session, we'll come back and go through the details.
I notice by your list here, you don't have 'Gone With The Wind'.
No.
'Gone With The Wind' was the very first record I made.
That's right. And it's listed under -- Claude Thornhill's name.
I see, that's right. It is.
Which is one of the reasons
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
why the discographic material (unintelligible) is a little bit confusing, because it does appear under so many people's names like Benny Carter, as I was saying before and Teddy Wilson.
Well, you know, "Gone With The Wind" was my very first accruity. And I hadn't reached the stature of getting a label of my own yet -- I mean a name of my own yet.
And, of course, you know that Claude at the time was managing me. And he had access to the studio. In fact, he was arranging for Andre Kostelanetz at the time.
At NBC, I think.
Yes. And I had been introduced to him by Gladys Mosier who is a pianist in Pittsburg.
So he set up this record date, and I recorded. And he had a male singer -- he's probably listed -- is it listed as "Dark As Ever"? What is it? "Harbor Lights." I don't know who the vocal --
Jimmy Farrell.
Jimmy Farrell. I didn't
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
even know him. I hadn't been in New York long enough to know any of these musicians.
So that was my introduction to the recording industry. And I believe on the label it says, 'Introducing Maxine Sullivan.'

And I just found out a few months ago -- and this was like forty-something years later -- that I heard the other side -- the other vocal that I did at the same time, 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart,' which was never released, that I know anything about.
Well I have a reference here (Vocalion) 3616. I'm not sure what the reverse~~ -- it was probably instrumental on the other side.
No, the vocal. The other vocalist. See, we were both recording the same day.
I see.
So, there were four sides made. I sang on two sides and Jimmy Farrell sang on the other two sides.
And I believe on the other side of 'Gone

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
With The Wind, was 'Harbor Lights.' So 'Whispers In The Dark' must've been on the other side of 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart.'
I see. Okay, would you like to play 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart?' And maybe we can --
I don't have 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart.'
I have it on my tape here.
You got it? I'd love to hear it.
(Tape Played.)
I don't think we mentioned that that was the 14th of June 1937 -- the date of that session was. You have any recollection about any of the musicians with you?
Well as I said before, I was so new in the city, I hadn't even had a chance to be introduced to all of the musicians that were around. But looking at this line-up here, we had
some pretty heavies here. Like Manny Klein, Charlie Spivack, Jack Lacey, Toots Mondello, Jess Carneol, Babe Russin. Babe Russin had made some records with me later. I knew him.
Eddie Powell, Claude Thornhill, of course. I thought when I heard this record a few months ago, 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart,' I didn't know that that was Claude.
But -- on vibes -- but I don't think that's vibes. I think that's more marimba because it had that wooden sound.
Yes, that's --
Artie Bernstein, bass -- I worked with him later. Chauncey Morehouse, Jimmy Farrell -- I didn't even know who the other vocalist was on that date.
Yes.

Because I never heard 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart' as a release. And when my son played it for me a couple of months ago, I listened. And all of a sudden, it dawned on me that it was my recording that I had made forty-something years
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yes, but you felt the title in your mind is "Gone With The Wind?"

Yes.
It came up because I -- as I said before -- I had just come to New York. I don't think I'd been in New York two months when that was made.
And I came to New York from Pittsburgh.
So the club that I was working in, I sent about ten copies back to Pittsburgh.
And I got a note that it was number one on their hit parade down there.

So, can we assume from what you say, that it wasn't a practice for record companies to make copies of the records available to the performers when they were issued? Because I do believe that "Stop, You're Breaking My Heart" did come out.

No, I mean --
In fact, I didn't even know that it was ever released. And, of course, "Gone With The Wind" -- on the other side of "Gone With The Wind" was

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Jimmy Farrell's vocal of 'Harbor Lights.' See, I wasn't on both sides.
Yes.
And the copy that I had, I had to go out and buy. Yes. Maybe they give away some now, but in those days, not particularly.
How about other economic considerations. You know how much they paid you and what the terms --
I don't know if I even got paid for that recording. The only one I remember getting paid for was the next one. You know, the one when I did 'Loch Lomond.'
Yes.
I didn't even get paid for that.
Okay. Well let's go and consider some of those titles now. And that was the second session you did, also for Vocalion, in which you recorded four titles on the 6th of August 1937.
So, off tape let's listen to those, okay?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Okay.
Okay, so now we come to a date which was the first date recorded under your name.
Yes.
And the titles are "Loch Lomond," your big hit; "I'm Coming Virginia," "Annie Laurie" and "Blue Skies."
Yes. Well you see, I had gone in to the Onyx Club to work at that time. In fact, when I first came to New York, I was doing intermission with a pianist by the name of Jennie Dillard.
She was your accompanist?

In Pittsburgh, yes. We came to New York together. Now when I went in to the Onyx Club, John Kirby was in there, but Kirby's band wasn't organized at the time. As you might recall, Stuff Smith had just closed the Onyx Club and he went on to the
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

west coast to appear at Famous Door.
So these groups of musicians that were
there -- Frankie Newton, Buster Bailey, Pete Brown,
Babe Russin, John Kirby and O'Neil Spencer -- well
I believed that the band at that particular point
was under the direction of Frankie Newton.
But Claude used these musicians on
my record date. And that happened to be the group
that was the Onyx at the time.

There's story that John
Kirby went uptown somewhere. Excuse me, went
downtown and got himself a contract to play on
52nd Street for a band he didn't have at the time.
So he went uptown and got the Frankie
Newton, Pete Brown --

That's quite possible.
No, but I think Frankie Newton was
already there because -- see, at the time the Onyx
Club, while the street itself was called the Cradle
of Swing, and all the musicians used to hang out down
there --
I should say, there's an

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
excellent tape recorded interview with you a short, called Swing Street.
Right. And since Frankie Newton had been down in the area, there was a group that was playing opposite Stuff, that Spirits of the Rhythm.
And then before theat, there was -- Jonah Jones was in there with Cozy Cole, that bunch.
Leo Watson.
Leo Watson, yes. So I think it was Frankie Newton's band up to the point when Kirby took over, see.
Because -- now O'Neil Spencer who was listed as a drummer on there -- Lucky Millinder's band was out of New York at the time. They were on the road. And when --
-- The Blue Rhythm Band.
That's right.
And actually, the only people that Kirby had with him at the time were Buster Bailey and O'Neil Spencer.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
When the bank came in town, then that's when he went and got Russell Procope and Charlie Shavers.
But this original record had Pete Brown who was very good alto man, and so was Babe Russin on tenor, and Claude, himself, on piano.
Yes.
So I think that Claude -- Well at the time, the reason that Claude selected 'Lock Lomond' was because --
That was his choice?
Yeah, uh huh -- and 'Annie Laurie.'
We felt that 'Annie Laurie' might make the hit. We had no idea that 'Lock Lomond' would do anything.
Can I ask you this? We'll come back, as I say, in the next interview to the Pittsburgh period of your life and so on, but did you sing either of those songs in Pittsburgh before you came to New York?
None of these.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
"Loch Lomond" and "Annie Laurie," specifically.

No. My big song in Pittsburgh -- that is, getting into the swing and the classy bit was "Trees". But we never recorded that.

You see, when I came to New York -- let's face it, you had a whole lot of singers here already. I think Claude was sort of wise to select these things like "Loch Lomond" and "Annie Laurie" -- was that at least make it a little different from just an average vocalist (singing) in front of the band.

And it isn't a novelty. Claude may have known what he was doing, because I knew from nothing -- I just went along for the ride.
So he really was responsible for decisions to use that material?
Oh yes.
I remember seeing in a periodical called "Rhythm," a short article on you by Leonard Feather. Maybe it was one of the first things written by you -- I think he said first you

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yes.
And then the decision to do 'Loch Lomond' came after that.
Claude actually thought that 'Annie Laurie' might be the one to click. I mean if you're looking for something to click. As it turned out, 'Loch Lomond' was the one.
Yes.
And, of course, you know it became quite controversial.
Indeed.
Yes. We would turn off the -- at the time there was a program on CBS called 'The Saturday Swing Club,' and Claude got me on the program.

I sang 'Loch Lomond' and -- Leo Fitzpatrick, station manager in Detroit, cut it off the air right in the middle of the song because he said it was sacrilegious to swing a traditional song. And then, of course, the following week, we did 'Loch Lomond' and these things on this side in
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
New York. And they had a group in Chicago -- they had Ray Heatherton and Reese Stevens with a big orchestra and a choir and everything singing 'Loch Lomond', and 'A Brown Bird Singing' straight.
And I was in New York with a small combination, (shivering). It ran on for quite a while.
There's also a record that you hear occasionally on the nostalgia stations of Martha Tilton.
Yes.
I think probably from the 1938 Carnegie Hall Concert of Benny Goodman.
Yeah, well you know how that happened.
You personally, were on the west coast at that time?
No. The band was on the road. And when Benny Goodman left the city, there was no such person as Maxine Sullivan around.
So while they were out on the road -- I imagined they stopped in some little town and put a nickle in the juke box and they heard this recording
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

of 'Loch Lomond.' So Jimmy Mundy took the arrangement off the record. And when they came to New York and did the concert at Carnegie Hall, and Martha Tilton sang it, you know, they thought they were introducing somebody, and I was singing it on second speed. So that got to be a big joke too, you know.
Yeah.
Even now, you hear --
Do you feel resentful about that?

No! I mean we knew what happened. It couldn't hurt. You know, the more recordings of 'Loch Lomond,' the more popular it was going to make me. And the controversy didn't hurt either. I left Leo Fitzpatrick years later, and I told him -- I said, 'You're the one who turned me off the air.' He said, 'Well it didn't hurt you a bit.' And it didn't.
Detroit's decision
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
we call a month or so I think.
Yes. Well it's sort of a crazy business because --
(Inaudible) about in DownBeat.
The college kids were responsible for it being a success because I was singing at the Onyx Club around summer months, during vacation. We had a college kids come in the Onyx Club at the time.
And they went for it. It was the novelty of it.
There was no stopping us after that.
There is one minor point we need to make about 'Look Limited.' That is, you're not exactly the only vocalist on it, are you?
No, but (inaudible). 'You take the high road and I'll take the low road.'
Yes. (Inaudible) Buster Bailey.
Yeah.
The other title that you

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
"I'm Coming Virginia."
Yes.
Which got me thinking when I was looking over this discography, it's an unusual song. And it's not the normal 32-bar chorus, but the construction is 24 bars, I think.
Yeah.
With three sections and --
Well "I'm Coming Virginia" was one of my own songs. That is, it's more of a thing that I had been doing, you know, previous to that.
"I'm Coming Virginia" has always been a favorite of mine. It's always been a good instrumental.

I think one of the first recordings I heard of it -- and this was even before I came to New York or thought I ever was going to do anything in show business, that Tea garden -- it's not a new -- it wasn't a new song.
Looking at my notes, I see it was written in 1927.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
That's right and --
It's one of those songs by a person who had one terrific song --
That's right.
(Inaudible) up again. It's on the table.
It has a good verse to, but at the time I wasn't doing any verses, just the vocal. And, of course, 'Blue Skies' is the standard. We try to keep it that way.
It wouldn't have been too good to have too much, say, gap between 'Lonesome' and whatever was currently popular. In fact, establish a standard repertoire.
These are things that I'm still doing. You know, forty years later, they're standards.
In fact, you've appeared quite often over the past ten -- more than that, isn't it? Fourteen years.
Yeah.
I guess you sing a --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yeah, when I sing 'I'm Coming Virginia' (unaudible).

Yeah, that's favorite. Okay. Now you went into the recording studio again this time for the Brunswick Label, accompanied by the Claude Thornhill Band again, 26th of August 1937. And it's 'Don't Save Your Love for a Rainy Day,' which --
I did?
-- charming.
I'd like to hear it.
Let's play it.
(Song Played.)
Okay, well how did that sound to you?
Oh boy. 'Don't Save Your Love for a Rainy Day' -- that's one I had completely forgotten about.
That must've been one of those dates that Claude had and he needed a singer, so he just reached out and grabbed me.
Well he couldn't have made a better choice. It was absolutely delightful.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
I think I'll put that back into my repertoire. It's a good song.
I wish you would.
Yeah.
Okay, also (Inaudible) While you're playing that, we also have more recollections and comments about "Locka Loemand."

Yeah. While I was listening to the vocal, you know, I remembered when I came to New York, Ella Fitzgerald was tops, and she still is as far as I'm concerned. But I think that there was a certain similarity between my style and hers. And, of course, it's nothing to wonder about that because we're all influenced by other singers. And, of course, Ella had been a favorite of mine because even back in Pittsburgh long before I ever thought I'd be coming to New York, I used to listen to Ella's recordings. And I also listened to the broadcast from the Savoy Ballroom. And so I would think that I might've been imitating Ella up to a certain point.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

However, it wouldn't done any of us any good for me to be trying to compete with Ella Fitzgerald. So I think that's one of the reasons why Claude reached out there and got "Lock Lowoud" and "Annie Laurie", to get me on another track.
If I was going to make it, I wouldn't be making it as a second Ella Fitzgerald. You know, you want to make it as one Maxine Sullivan.
But that had a curious repercussion you were just saying also.
Yes.
It caused Ella to modify her repertoire.
Yeah. Ella admits that up until I did "Lock Lowoud" that she really didn't have -- I guess you would call it a gimmick -- something to identify with.
And so, after I did Lock Lowoud and it got to be such a big novelty thing, then they went out and wrote "A Tiskit A Tasket" for Ella. She admits that herself.
And "Chew Chew Your Chewing
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Gum?
Yeah, and those kind of things.
And possibly she did rather better before. I mean, there's a beautiful song she made with Teddy Wilson in 1936 which I love. It's called "All My Life."
Oh yes, sure:
Is that a big hit --
I heard they were. So far, (inaudible) listen to recordings, you know, nine times out of ten everything that that particular person makes, they're going to like.

But you need one song. I remember hearing one of Ella's old records, Rhythm and Romance, which I loved. In fact, all of us here have done quite a few recordings before I even thought about coming to New York.
In fact, in Pittsburgh -- I'm actually from Homestead, Pennsylvania which is a little small town outside of Pittsburgh -- and I happened to belong to a club called the "Prosperity Club." And we had
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

a dance -- we promoted a dance -- and for some reason or other, the band -- the Chick Webb Bank -- had been playing in Pittsburgh at one of the theaters. And it was their last night and they were closing. I don't know how we happened to get them, except for the fact that we had a very dynamic president of the club who could get just about anything she wanted.
Do you remember what year this was?

It had to be 1932. In fact, I have an autographed book with Ella's autograph in it, and she doesn't even know if she signed it. But I was waiting tables during the affair. And all of a sudden I heard this voice and I knew it was Ella Fitzgerald. I didn't wait tables the rest of the night. I went and sat right in front of the bad. And I think this was one of the first tours that Ella was out on. This was right after she first got started. And it was Chick Webb's band.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And incidentally, John Kirby was playing the bass with the band that night. And Clift Jackson was here on the piano, because I got both of their autographs.
I didn't know one musician from the other at that time. We had a lot of bands coming through.
Okay. Well I've seen reference to that story in the line notes, the album, John Kirby on the bass, on Columbia.
There you say it around 1934?
I think it was 1932 because I have the -- my autograph book. Well this is later. This date is wrong. It should be 1932.
Okay. I hope --
You really can't remember those dates sometimes.
Yes, I know.

We've been talking about Ella Fitzgerald. Billy Holiday's name come to my mind in connection with looking for the genesis of 'Lotta Lownonda', because I believe on her first record dates, she cut a song
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
called "Riffing Scotch."
Yeah?
Do you remember that?
No, I don't.
(inaudible) Claude Thornhill may have gotten the idea -- may have triggered something, or that was part of some --

Actually the time that I did Lock Loehman, I think one of the first efforts -- I'm pretty sure they've been swinging classics forever -- you know, bands (inaudible) as a novelty -- but Tommy Dorsey had just recorded "Song of India," and the interest seemed to have in that direction of swing, you know, picking up some old things -- classics or whatever. And given them the swing treatment. I understand -- In fact, after I did Lock Loewend and it became such a sensation on the street, Ella Logan appeared one night with a bunch of Scotsmen in (inaudible) picketing the (inaudible) because I was doing "Lock Loewend." And I understand that she did
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
She made -- I guess you get a press release or something that -- which would appear in DownBeat --

Well I think she probably had -- because Ella Logan was definitely in New York singing before I got here. And she appeared on some of the swing programs. I'm sure she must've done 'Loch Lomond.' That could -- I don't know whether that was the reason Claude selected it or not. But I do know that she got very upset.
Here we are -- I just found a Xerox of it. It's DownBeat's April 1938, and here's a picture of Ella Logan.
Yeah, uh huh, yeah. Well I always say that there was nothing unusual about a Scots girl singing a Scot song, but when I did it --
Anyway, a couple of months later, I think --
Yes, that was right after --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
There was a big interview with --
Yeah, well this helped, you know.
So it didn't hurt.
Not a bit. Not a bit.
Okay. Let's move on to the 22nd of October 1937.
What did I do then?
This was a vocal date, It's "Easy to Love", "The Folks Who Lived On The Hill."
Another song with a rather unusual structure and rather a traditional song by "Darling Nellie Gray" -- and It's "Nice Work If You Can Get It."

"Easy To Love" and "Nice Work If You Can Get It" did wind up on the DownBeat poll for the release of the week -- you know, that they ran it every week. And I think "Nice Work If You Can Get It" and "Easy To Love" both ran first and second, and second and first for about a month.
So I had gotten that far getting listed.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

And, of course, I always liked "The Folks Who Live On The Hill." And, of course, "Darling Nellie Gray" was more in keeping with the traditional style that he had established by doing the early "Loch Lomond" and "Annie Laurie" thing.
And these were all, of course, Claude Thornhill's selections, because he was my mentor.
In fact, while the news was getting around, Archer Winston who was a critic for one of the newspapers -- he hadn't really got into hearing Maxine Sullivan.
But I guess the news got around, and it was a very big spread in the paper -- I think it was the Telegraph.
It said "Modern Svengali Discovers Sepia (inaudible)." Twilby?
Oh.
So that didn't hurt either. We made headlines then.
But Claude was really responsible for other those/things. He was pretty hard with me because, number one, he had the connections; he had been around
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
for a long time and he had making recordings. And he was really pushing me, you know.
Claude wasn't a booking agent. He was strictly a musician, you see. And he -- I supposed he liked what I was doing. So he worked on it.
And he tried very hard. In fact, there's no doubt about it -- I mean, after I did 'Loch Lomond.' I did become a big success on the Street.
And Claude used to come and sit outside the club on the curb and cry while the crowd was coming in. He was quite happy about that.
So he --
Is that literally true or --
That is true! That is true!

You know, just about that time, the Columbia put the Saturday Swing Club on the stage at Loew's State live, along with some other acts -- Les Lieber who plays a (inaudible) was playing a penny whistle.
Right now, he heads an organization called
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
"Jazz At Noon."
Oh yes.

You know, Les Lieber. So Les Lieber was on that bill. And he was playing his penny whistle there. And some other acts which I don't quite remember, but Leith Stevens was the band and Paul Douglas was the announcer. In fact, on the air when the program came on, Paul Douglas would say, "The Saturday Night Swing Club is now is session." So Columbia decided to put this on the stage at Loew's State. And while we were playing there that week, an article came out in the New Yorker. And it was about -- the New Yorker had interviewed some woman -- I don't remember her name -- from Great Britain who played the (inaudible). And they had a profile on her. And at the end of her interview, they asked her what she wanted to do while she was in the United States. And she said she wanted to hear "Annie Laurie" and Loch Lomond whom she had heard God knows where.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Well up until that time, Joe Helbock who was the owner of -- the operator of the Onyx Club -- he didn't think too much of what was happening. He was still trying to get Stuff Smith from the west coast.
But anyway, after he saw this article in the New Yorker, then they blew up by picture, put it out front, and called the New Yorker and said, 'You don't have to worry, here she is.'
It goes back farther than that. When I -- I met Gladys Mosier in Pittsburgh while I was working at the Benjamin Harris Literary Club.
And Gladys was the pianist of Ina Ray Hutton's band. So she had mentioned that --
Well, I mean all the musicians when they played Pittsburgh would wind up at the Benjamin Harris Literary Club because it was an after hours spot. And I got a lot of encouragement there.
But Gladys said, if you ever come to New York, look me up. So I had no address or anything like that. This was just a stroke of luck.
I came to New York -- I got off from work
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

like a Sunday Morning -- I came to New York on a Sunday excursion. And Jennie Dillard's brother -- he lived here in New York so he listened to the story, and he said he'd be looking for Gladys Mosier.
It was just by luck the band was playing at the Paramount Theater. I mean, this has got to be luck.
Did you buy a round-trip ticket?
Yes, I still have the other half. Oh yeah.

In fact, I didn't bring anything with me but a cake of soap and a towel. When I left, the only person that knew I was coming to New York was the waiter. His name was Obie, at the club. And he was a fan of mine. He was responsible for bringing a lot of musicians up there to hear me.
And I told him -- I said, "Look, I'm going to New York. And if I make it, I won't be back. But if I don't make it, I'll be back Monday night."
So, he was the only one that knew that I had gone. We finally found out that Gladys was at
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
the theater. We talked with her on the phone. I called her up and told her where I was, and she said, "Maxine who?" She didn't remember. It had been maybe six months, or more than that.
Were you using the name Sullivan?

There was alot of promotion from "My Old Friends" and I did alot of talk - I went on the air, radio and television, you know, to help promote the show. And being a senior too, a senior citizen there are allot of shows, "Over Easy" especially.
You've been twice on that?
Yeah, twice. The first time I
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

did the show I sang "There's Still A Little Starch Left In The Old Girl Yet". I did the one song and we discussed the show and also a bit about my efforts in the community. And so I was invited back again just a few weeks ago in September to do "Over Easy" again. I flew out to San Francisco and the theme of that show was 'Volunteers'. Mainly about what I'm doing now community-wise. Right now the South Bronx seems to be in the news and they know about the South Bronx and so I guess they wanted to know how you survive in the South Bronx and how come I'm still here, you know. And I sang "They All Laughed" and "A Hundred Years From Today" on the show.
What did you tell them about how to survive in the South Bronx?

I said to get involved. I mean, everybody is not going to get up and leave. We've lost quite a few people. We lost alot of the population and anybody that comes to the Bronx, I mean, you know, they figure this is like Germany after the war. The devestation. You got abandoned buildings here and vacant lots, buildings that have been torn down. At one time here there was fire like every fifteen minutes. It was enough to frighten anybody.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

I've been living here in the same house for thirty-five years and I don't feel like I want to go anyplace. I like it here and I got alot of friends here, and some of the community work I've done here. I feel like, well where am I going? It isn't that easy to pick up and go. So that's what I talked about. And then I told them about to what extent I was involved in the community at this particular point, you know, I established The House That Jazz Built a few years ago and it's a project that I'm very much interested in and working with and making some headway. I'm going to be doing some things this year or this winter or up until spring of 1981 through the New York City Youth Board and the Board of Education. We're going to take programs sponsored by The House That Jazz Built into a school, an after-school program. And I'll be working with kids from the age group 7 to 14 and 14 to 19 years old. And our program is geared to meeting improvement through the study of one hundred years of jazz. So I don't, know how much they're going to improve in their reading but they're going to know a whole lot of new terms. But it looks very good. I'm very happy about it and I think we're
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

going to have a lot of fun. And we intend to involve the kids very much so I think there's a lot of talent in the area and the Bronx seems to be like out of everything. We want them to know the Bronx is here. We have a lot of musicians who live in the Bronx but they take their talents down-town. After all, down-town is the Apple but the Bronx is part of the apple too. Well it is now, we just might pull out any minute and become part of the mainland. We are the only borough that's connected to the mainland. So we might secede. Anyway I moved here in 1945. I liked it because it was residential. It's not that I was very busy working down-town. I - when I moved here I had been all over the City looking for some-place to live, Brooklyn, Long Island, and then I found this house and I'm a half hour at the most down-town on the subway. And it couldn't be anymore convenient. And then it was a wonderful place to raise kids when Paula was a little girl. And so I was lucky. I found this little house. As I said before, this house used to belong to Eddie Mallory who at one time was a musician. And also was married to Ethel Waters. Although he wasn't married to her when I moved here. But I found
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

a lot of Ethel Waters recordings here. I think the very first recording she ever made was here because I bought the house furnished. I have one of the first records she made of "Am I Blue". It's a blue record. And some of her earlier, Dianh Swan records.
"Am I Blue" was from Blackbirds?
No, "Am I Blue" was just a single tune.
Oh, "I Must Have That Man", that's the one I'm thinking of, sorry.
"Am I Blue" was a single that she made. I found quite a few things here that she made. So I'm here and I'm staying.
And The House That Jazz Built, that was Cliff Jackson?

Yeah, well the House That Jazz Built was a little building that we bought in 1956. And when we first had it, well first of all, Orville, my son was going to music school and I set it up so he would have a little studio over there. And there was a space over there for some of the musicians that were in and out of town. That was a place for them to leave their

trunk, and they had sort of a little dorm over there. Vic And/Dickenson lived there. Marcus Foster, Ron Scott, Jimmy Rainey, and in fact the Meade "Lux" Lewis stayed there on one of his engagements in New York. He stayed at the house and the night that he got killed he had just left from The House That Jazz Built. So after the guys, most of them got settled with apartments of their own - and then of course, there was nobody living there. This was Cliff's baby, you know. He went over and saw the boys every day and sort of kept the house up. But when the guys left we didn't have anybody staying there so a local anti-poverty program moved in there. And they were in there for three or four years. In the meantime Cliff passed in 1970 and I found myself in charge. By this time the house was in sort of a dilapidated state of affairs and I had to get those people out so I got together with Wilma Dobie, Dobey's, a friend of mine, and I had this idea in the back of my head for a long time. Anyway, I didn't have any idea of what we were going to call it so I came up with this thing, The House That Jazz Built. So in 1970, that's when we started thinking about it and we got the people out. In 1975 we had a dedication
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

The House That Jazz Built in memory of Cliff Jackson. And so for the past five years we've had summer programs in there for kids. We expose them to jazz and listen to records, take them out on trips, take them to jazz concerts. And it's my feeling that they just don't know their enough about jazz roots and so this is what we're going to try to do from now on in with the new program. And we've selected a pretty big piece of American History. We re calling it a Hundred Years Of Jazz, from 1880 to 1980. And I think in this way they may be able to relate a little bit to history because when you consider that I'll be dealing with kids seven years old, that means that they were born in 1971. They wouldn't know anything about the swing era, boogie-woogie, bop and they are into their thing now. I'm just wondering whose going to win, me or them, because I'm going to have to listen to more of their music then they have to listen to mine. But I think the tie-in, the Board of Education, I mean, we will be working with kids that are potential delinquents or maybe truants and things like that. This might be some way of getting them interested in getting them to go back to school. That's our aim. Is to get
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

them back into school. There's another problem too. We don't feel that there's enough activity for these kids from the time they get out of school, that is, constructive type activity. So for four hours . . .
Especially if the mother is working.

That's right. So when the kids get out of school, from three to five, these seven to fourteen year old kids will be in our program. And of course the older kids, well it's a choice for them. They like to have fun too. They're going to be very much involved. I mean, there might be some kids out here with some talent which we hope to promote. I don't know how many kids are into music. I'm pretty sure there are some music programs in the school and these kids can play an instrument, we can get them into jazz. We can get some of our jazz bands to come up and sit in with them. This is not entirely impossible. I have a feeling that if there are kids up here that are interested that they are probably taking private lessons. But even so, this would be an ideal opportunity for them to get a chance to rehearse. They may not be allowed to practice
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

at home. I ran into a little boy, thirteen years old and he's into a program and he has been suspended because he didn't do so well and he's - he doesn't have access to his instrument. And so I told him to practice with his mouth piece, play the trumpet, and he said that even when he had the horn, which is the school's property-they don't exactly allow them to bring the instruments home. But on the occasions when he could his parents didn't want him practicing because, you know, a kid practicing in your house. So anyway this is going to be a thing. I'm very happy about it and I'm thinking that we're going to win.
Well I certainly hope so. I wish you every success with it.
Yes. By June of 1981 you're going to be hearing from us. We got it all planned. You're going to really be involved. I'm not going to give away my secrets now, but come back in June.
Okay.
Just hang in there because I hope you'll come and sit in on us and see what we're doing, you know. It's a challenge.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yeah, okay. Would you say at this point that this is your essential interest?

Yeah, definitely. I mean my singing career it's second nature to me now. You know, they call me and I can go and do something. I can do no wrong, you know. So you're going to do something that challenges you and this is it. And I really feel that there is something missing so far as the kids are concerned. You see when I was young, listen, I guess I was singing every time I got a chance. There's no place for these kids to try their ways. You're either on top or not at all. And of course the business itself, I mean, I was lucky, I was discovered. I didn't have any money when I came to New York. But now you got kids that if they want to get into show business they got to start out with about forty thousand dollars or you know, get an angel. And by the time he makes the first forty thousand dollars somebody else has the money and he has had it. His career is over. This is the truth.
Yes.
So we got to get a proving ground for them. And who knows, they don't have to be

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
interested in a career but I think that everybody ought to have a chance to do their thing.
Sure.
And in front of an audience. There are no more amateur nights.
Yeah, you're going to do something along those lines for these kids?

Oh yeah, if possible. I mean there are a couple of theatres in the neighborhood showing horror pictures. We might get the kids on stage, you know what I mean, and have some live - we might even bring back vaudeville. I doubt it but at least we can have some fun.
Okay. So in terms of your singing, how do you view your career say over the next few years. Are you going to be doing pretty much the same thing?

Yeah, I'll be getting calls you know. When I was first considered for this particular program I said, you know, like a couple of days a week like a couple of hours I would do it. But the idea seems to have gained certain amount of momentum and so

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
it wound up being three days, four hours a day which is twelve hours a week.
That's right.
It's Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. I can still do my weekends but I just can't take any extended engagements.
Well, you have done that haven't you? You were in Atlantic City for instance, during August.

Yeah, that's the last until June of 1981. But I will be doing weekends or whatever comes up. I decided that I would take the time out to do this. And I don't really like to get away that much anyway. And I can satisfy my career on a Friday or a Saturday night, you know, just get out once in awhile. and mingle with the musicians and things like that. So that's enough for me. And look at the fun I'm going to be having with 120 kids. There's got to be some talent out there someplace.
Well that's more than I could handle.
I'm going to have my hands
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

full but I'm going to have allot of cooperation. There are allot of parents who'd like to see their kids do something. And listen, I'm working with seniors and they're enjoying it, so you never get too old for music. And the kids, you know, I don't know where they came from or how they got to where they are, so that's what we're going to tell them. I got, I mean all the musicians that I see I tell them what's happening and they say, well call on me so I want to have old models for them, and I want to have guests in and they can talk to them. If these kids are thinking in the wrong direction we just might be able to put them on the right track because the musicians, they paid allot of dues and I think they'd be the first ones to tell them what not to do.

You know the House That Jazz Built has a membership of about 150 people scattered nationally and we have a local board consisting of musicians and people that are especially interested in jazz. We have four jazz parties a year and we have one coming up, Sunday October the 19th. Of course, this is one of the means that we have used to raise funds to carry out the program at The House That Jazz Built. And it's an on-going thing.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

So we're looking forward to a good time and one of the young ladies that's going to perform for us, three years ago she worked at The House That Jazz Built under a Jobs For Youth Progam while she was still going to school. And now she's a talent in her own rank. We didn't develop that talent but maybe a little bit of us rubbed off on her. And they call themselves "Born To Be-Bop" and they're going to be doing things . . .
This is a group?

A group, yes. There are seven of them, two girl singers and five musicians. And their repertoire consists of songs by Louie Jordan and Louie Armstrong, so I think that maybe we're getting through to some of them, in all ways.
Yes. That sounds interesting. Who else will be performing?

Well, Alan Hanlon is guitar player. He's one of our Board Members and he's our regular musical director. And the other, young lady with whom I met at one of the performances that I did for the senior citizens, she's got a group of young people and they're going to model fashions. So we hope it's going

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

to be real great. And I spoke to a friend of mine and I'm keeping my fingers crossed that I think we'll be able to televise this so we'll have something we can show a little later on, about what The House That Jazz Built is really doing. Of course, we have the regulars. I always sing whether anybody asks me or not.
Is it going to be at N.Y.U. Law School?

Yeah, N.Y.U. School of Law. At our last Jazz Party, which was our annual meeting in July, we had Carmen Leggio and Flossie, I forget Flossie's last name, but he plays the tenor and she plays the trumpet and flute. And they're going to play for us. And allot of the musicians from Ryans promised that they would drop in and sit in, so we always have some extra guests. We tell them to bring their axes. And of course we serve a little wine and snacks and have a combination meeting and jazz concert. And the proceeds are used to buy supplies or some of the things we need at The House That Jazz Built, I mean, at this new program because we're not - certain funds are not available for administrative purposes and we'll need to set up some kind of
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

an administration. So we'll raise the funds ourselves. And there's one thing that I mainly want to do, in the room that we have there's no piano there so we're negotiating for an electronic piano. So the funds that we get from the jazz party will be used for that. That's the main thing we'll get because it has something for the kids. And it has to be portable because the space that we're using, we have to clear in and clear out each time we use it. So a portable piano is just the thing we need.
You're not actually doing this at the House.

No this program will be conducted in a school, Community School 50, in the Bronx, and I have a very nice room and I'll be able to handle 120 kids. Well, there'll be 60 at a time, from seven to fourteen, and 60 from fourteen and a half to nineteen.
That's a tribute to your energy and your courage to take on that.
I'm going to have alot of help.
I don't the average size of the school classes are these days but school teachers don't
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

They want it down to fifteen. No, I can break this group up into four, four different little groups. In fact, the seven-to-fourteen group, I'm going to divide that into like kids from seven to eleven and eleven to fourteen. You got to consider the age difference too. You know fourteen year olds don't want to be hanging out with seven year olds, and vice-verser. And the other age group, I'd break that down too into two groups, thirty apiece. So, no problem.
Well, I wish you lots of luck.
We're going to have fun.

Well with that we come to the end of the sixth and final interview session. I want to thank you very much indeed Maxine Sullivan for the excellent material you've given us, and I want to wish you the very best of success in your future project. Thank you.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
