segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: One-night stand tour with Benny Carter
segments.summary: Her only tour of one-night stands; six weeks from July from New York as far south and to Detroit.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Le Ruban Bleu, Herbert Jacobi and the supper club concept
segments.summary: She worked six years at Le Ruban Bleu, an east-side supper club run by Herbert Jacobi, with a new around-the-clock format.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Decca arrangements by Peter van Steeden and early difficulties recording
segments.summary: During that time it was difficult to make records; Decca arrangements were by Peter van Steeden.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: The Benny Carter sides of 1941
segments.summary: Discussion of 'What a Difference a Day Makes' and other Carter sides she hasn't heard in years.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Decca sessions of December 1941 and January 1942
segments.summary: Why four sides were unissued and re-recorded; confusion over which titles exist.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: March 1942 Decca session with a studio group
segments.summary: They listen to 'Beside the River Clyde'; Maxine says the discographies are wrong and the date was put together by Decca, not Billy Kyle.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: The ASCAP strike, Charlie Shavers and clean broadcasts
segments.summary: On the ASCAP situation and her classical-jazzing, and Charlie Shavers quoting tunes in solos on the show.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Recording drought and the Joe Davis sides
segments.summary: She wasn't in demand and then recorded for Joe Davis with Herman Chittison's trio members including Barksdale.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Strings and a missing trumpet on the Joe Davis session
segments.summary: Hughes sorts out discographical errors: no trumpet or tenor on the date, with piano, bass, guitar and strings.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Whether those sides were meant as hits, and who approached her to record
segments.summary: She says it was just a date, not a hit-seeking one, and she was approached by different people after coming off the road.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Teddy Wilson date, January 1945
segments.summary: She sings a pair of sides on Teddy Wilson's date with Charlie Shavers.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Deluxe date reunited with Benny Carter, January 1946
segments.summary: Benny got in touch with her for the session.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: The New Friends of Rhythm sides for International
segments.summary: Sylvan Shulman's group, studio musicians with advanced, odd arrangements; date probably 1947.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Choosing her own material, 'Mad About the Boy' and getting tired of folk songs
segments.summary: She selected the songs herself, wanted to stretch out, and was tired of being identified with folk-song swing.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Le Ruban Bleu, Herman Chittison and unrecorded club work
segments.summary: She stayed six years at Le Ruban Bleu working with great musicians; much of her best work there was never taped.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: The Ellis Larkin trio album, her best, and poor pressings
segments.summary: She worked with Ellis Larkin on the International album, judges it her best, but poor vinyl made the needle skate.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Reissue ideas for the Larkin album and a memorial album
segments.summary: Hughes and Maxine discuss rights, Monmouth-Evergreen, and a forty-two-song memorial album Phil Schaap might help with.

segments.chapter: Kirby, Decca and postwar recordings
segments.title: Apollo and MGM sides of 1948
segments.summary: The Apollo sides 'Cry Buttercup, Cry' and 'Restless' are a mystery; the MGM pair she sang nowhere else.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Second trip to England and the 1954 recordings with Vic Ash
segments.summary: She recalls a tour with Ralph Sharon and recording 'Pipe in the Glen' and a Maxixe tune for Parlophone.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Recording with British musicians; singing in London
segments.summary: She enjoyed the British musicians; Hue magazine's photo essay on her singing in London in 1954.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: 'Loch Lomond' controversy in Britain
segments.summary: In 1948 she went to the UK; the English resented the swing Loch Lomond more than the Scots.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Touring the British Isles in 1948: Cardiff and the Royal Theater
segments.summary: She toured to Wales, played Cardiff and the Royal Theater, and had a great reception.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Staying with Adelaide Hall in London
segments.summary: Adelaide Hall's big house, mostly closed up, in postwar London.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: American acts in postwar London and rationing
segments.summary: She worked the London Casino with American acts and recalls ration packages and a feast with a friend.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Length of her stays and the north: Ireland, Dundee
segments.summary: She stayed about sixty days in one place, enjoyed Dublin, a steak, and Scotland's hospitality.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: End of the first session, location and start of the second
segments.summary: Hughes closes the first session at The House That Jazz Built in the Bronx and opens the second on 21 July 1980.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Bernice Reape's story of adding a middle to 'Prelude to a Kiss'
segments.summary: A visitor tells how she added a bridge to Ellington's tune at his apartment, then heard it on the radio; she now studies harmony.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: The Rutgers visit and hearing 'Stop, You're Breaking My Heart' again
segments.summary: Maxine's mini-tour at Rutgers on 17 July and her reaction when her son played the old record.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Dating 'Going Places' and the outtake record from Joe Franklin
segments.summary: Searching books and David Chertok for facts on the movie dates and a record of cut songs like 'Say It with a Kiss'.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Soundies and other film appearances
segments.summary: Her voice was heard in other movies and Soundies, including the Benny Carter short and Dorothy Dandridge's scenes.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: An error in a French jazz-in-film book
segments.summary: The caption wrongly places her in a film that doesn't exist; confusion with 'Swingin' the Dream'.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Gulliver's in Paterson and talk with Art Vincent and Al Pryor
segments.summary: Her Newark radio appearance, the Paterson club, and a conversation about musicians' plight and neglected recordings.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Stock arrangements of 'Loch Lomond' and the Benny Goodman copy
segments.summary: Jimmy Mundy took the arrangement from her record; the published stock arrangement had Goodman's arrangement credited.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Frank Schiffman and the Apollo Theater circuit
segments.summary: Schiffman owned the Apollo and the next stop was the Howard Theater; the black theater circuit.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Schiffman's control of the Apollo circuit and the West End Theater
segments.summary: She recounts how Schiffman shut a rival theater by cutting off acts, which owed him money and needed his booking.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Her run-in with Schiffman over booking with John Kirby at the Apollo
segments.summary: She skipped an Apollo opening billed with Kirby because she was newly remarried, and Schiffman retaliated; she never played the Apollo again.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: Why Claude Thornhill was in California; his arranging gifts
segments.summary: Hughes checks Claude's whereabouts; Maxine praises his blending of brass and reeds and his skeleton arrangements.

segments.chapter: Britain and second-session leftovers
segments.title: 'Boogie Woogie Maxixe' and the Vic Ash session in London
segments.summary: They settle the word as a Portuguese dance and correct the discography.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Transition to long-playing records and sorting the Period albums
segments.summary: Hughes and Maxine try to straighten out the three Period LPs and the Jazztone reissue.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: 'Flow Gently, Sweet Rhythm' as theme and the Kirby compositions
segments.summary: She explains the signature tune and how Charlie Shavers wrote most of the band's originals, linking to 'Opus de Funk'-like themes.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The Jazztone reissue mix-up and Leonard Feather's reunion album
segments.summary: Jazztone mixed tracks from separate sessions; Leonard Feather reunited Kirby alumni to revive the sound; they plan to write Feather and Bethlehem.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Kirby arrangements kept in the players' heads; a possible tribute
segments.summary: After the band broke up, arrangements lived in the musicians' heads; Al Cobb could transcribe them for a repertory project.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The later Kirby band, the bass clarinet and personnel losses
segments.summary: Later years used tenor players; Kirby bought a bass clarinet around 1939; losing three of five hurt the sextet.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Columbia's artist bureau, Sonny Werblin and MCA vaudeville dates
segments.summary: When Columbia gave up its bureau she dealt with Sonny Werblin and MCA, with disappointing theater dates in a few cities.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Footnote on 'Opus de Funk' and Charlie Shavers's 'Swedish Schapps'
segments.summary: Hughes traces the theme resembling Opus de Funk to Horace Silver and a Shavers composition.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The Andy Razaf tribute album on Period
segments.summary: She discusses the album for Andy Razaf, Leonard Feather's idea, missing tracks in the discography, its low-budget release, and hopes for reissue.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The 1958 concert recording and Billie Holiday's appearance
segments.summary: She sang 'Loch Lomond' and 'I'm Beginning to See the Light' on the 'Seven Ages of Jazz' album and recalls a sick Billie doing 'Lover Man'.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Manassas Jazz Festival and ending her retirement
segments.summary: In 1966 she sang a couple of songs at Manassas, Virginia, with Cliff Jackson, after years away because of raising her daughter.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The Town Hall concert of 1967
segments.summary: A caller from Town Hall proposed a concert; she asked Cliff to assemble the group.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Her return and the revival of mainstream jazz
segments.summary: She feels her comeback played a part in the upsurge of mainstream jazz after years when swing went underground; the traditionalist-versus-modernist split.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Hearing bebop and Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: In the mid-1950s she listened to Dizzy at the Royal Roost and wasn't impressed at first, but accepts it created a new sound.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Why she took up the valve trombone
segments.summary: She wanted an instrument to play; seeing Bob Brookmeyer and Billy Eckstine, she chose valve trombone and Cliff found one at Manny's.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Learning the valve trombone and being forced to play it
segments.summary: The beautiful horn lay around until the band called her up on a bandstand; she practiced a year for a concert in South Bay.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: John Wilson's review: 'stick to singing'
segments.summary: After the concert the critic wrote she played trombone like she sings but should stick to singing, which discouraged her.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The Hawaii trip, illness and retirement from singing
segments.summary: She went to Hawaii at the end of 1956, was sick after returning, and did not resume a singing career in 1957.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Switching to the flugelhorn
segments.summary: After work on her teeth she took to the flugelhorn, citing Miles Davis and Clark Terry, and carried it around hoping to play.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: The pocket trumpet from Bill Ratzenberger and sitting in with Clark Terry
segments.summary: She talked a pocket trumpet out of a Connecticut music-store owner and surprised Clark Terry at a concert by joining the blues.

segments.chapter: LP era, retirement and comeback
segments.title: Salute to Women in Jazz, Cobi Narita and playing on Broadway
segments.summary: At a women-in-jazz week the club owner locked out the group, so they played in the street at 53rd and Broadway.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: 'The Music of Hoagy Carmichael' with Bob Wilber
segments.summary: Bob Wilber and producer Bill Borden heard her at the Riverboat and used her on a Monmouth-Evergreen Carmichael album with members of the World's Greatest Jazz Band.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Choosing songs for 'Closest Pages in the Book'
segments.summary: Her album with Wilber, including 're-recording 'Gone With the Wind', 'Darn That Dream' and 'Too Many Tears'.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: 'Restless' and 'Harlem Butterfly' and the puzzling Mercer sheet music
segments.summary: She learned 'Restless' at Le Ruban Bleu; the sheet music credits puzzle them, as does a cover with Julie London.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: 'Every Time I Fall in Love', scat chorus and 'Loch Lomond'
segments.summary: She describes an old song worked out with Wilber, a scat chorus, and the album's repertoire including 'As Long As I Live'.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Fat Cat McRee's live Manassas albums and Tommy Gwaltney's group
segments.summary: How live festival recordings get taped and released, with musicians Fat Cat brings in, many from Blues Alley.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Titles on the 'Queen of Song' album; Claude Hopkins and 'I Thought About You'
segments.summary: Songs on the album, the traditional set with Claude Hopkins, and memories tied to 'I Thought About You'.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The proposed State Department tour and Blues Alley
segments.summary: Tommy Gwaltney contacted her about a tour that didn't happen; she praises Blues Alley and the Manassas festival.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The December 1969 Manassas album
segments.summary: Fat Cat tapes everything; she appeared with two groups and was working with Bobby Hackett in Boston when the album came out.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Rights, consignment and artists selling their own albums
segments.summary: How the festival recordings' rights are given up, flat fees, and artists selling albums themselves.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Bobby Hackett tracks and choosing material for festival records
segments.summary: Working with Bobby is a pleasure; she explains why few of her new songs appear on festival albums and why she picks uncommon material.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The Holland record and why she digs back for old songs
segments.summary: She did 'Something to Remember You By' in Holland; she avoids currently popular songs, and the overlap between jazz and pop has gone.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Overseas Press Club concert album with Earl Hines
segments.summary: A lunchtime concert at the Press Club with Earl Hines, whom she knew from Pittsburgh and saw with Louis Armstrong's group in 1952.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Her uncle's band in Homestead and her first taste of show business
segments.summary: Her uncle Harry led a band in Homestead that recorded on Gennett and let her sing; through him she got a first job.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Songs on the 1970 album: 'They All Laughed' and 'He's Funny That Way'
segments.summary: She explains choosing old songs, 'They All Laughed' from her early Onyx Club days, and running out of material.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The Shakespeare jazz album with Dick Hyman
segments.summary: Compared with Cleo Laine's Shakespeare record, Dick Hyman's arrangements were originally made for Earl Wrightson and the album used Rusty Dedrick, Bucky Pizzarelli and Milt Hinton.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: 'Take, Oh Take Those Lips Away' and the educational reaction
segments.summary: She favors the ballad version; educators wrote that the album could make Shakespeare palatable.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Pride in the album; why she doesn't perform it live
segments.summary: She can't improve on it but won't play it for audiences who swing it, and recalls Dick Hyman's declaiming at a presentation.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Singing men's songs and why she avoids other singers' songs
segments.summary: She says the Shakespeare songs were sung by men and women could do them, and discusses not encroaching on others' material, with Martha Tilton.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Who influenced her and whether anyone imitated her
segments.summary: She says nobody identified her style with anyone, citing Adelaide Hall and wordless vocals with Ellington.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Seeing touring shows, bands and TOBA acts in Pittsburgh
segments.summary: As a girl she saw road shows, dance bands, Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, the Elmore Theater and midnight shows.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Carnegie Hall concert recording with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: A concert for the Visiting Nurse association where she and Bobby Hackett were guests, accompanied by a quartet.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Touring with the World's Greatest Jazz Band and the Dutch connection
segments.summary: Ted Easton heard her at the concert, which led to the Holland album; she tours with the band.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Nice Jazz Festival tribute to Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: She appeared at Newport and Nice with the band; the unveiling of Louis's bust in Nice.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The Beaver Harris album, 1975
segments.summary: Beaver Harris, from Homestead, asked her to sing two songs on his 360 Degree Music Experience album; she sings 'Can There Be Peace'.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The Holland album with Ted Easton's jazz band
segments.summary: She stayed after the tour to record in a studio with Ted Easton, felt stranded, and sang songs from copies in her case.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Atlantic Club recordings in Stockholm
segments.summary: Two albums recorded live at the Atlantic Club, with Peanuts Hucko and a trumpeter she thinks was Billy Butterfield.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The Atlantic Club and Swedish club life
segments.summary: She describes the club, its membership, its owner Bo, and the contrast with younger clubs.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: How American musicians tour Europe and local rhythm sections
segments.summary: Musicians go club to club and are treated well; local players are good, though audiences vary.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Copenhagen, a Swedish television show and her 65th birthday
segments.summary: Only one night in Copenhagen, a lukewarm response, and a televised show in Stockholm where she celebrated her 65th birthday.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: 'We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye' for George Buck
segments.summary: How she was drawn to record in North Carolina, with Art Hodes and young players, and the bass saxophone.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: The George Buck album musicians and repertoire
segments.summary: She names the players and notes only a couple of songs she had recorded before; she can slip in unusual material.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Other albums in the works: Art Hodes group and Doc Cheatham
segments.summary: A small-group Art Hodes album, a Doc Cheatham date, and a Buck session including 'Brother, Can You Spare a Dime'.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Preferring small rhythm sections, and the limits of her early records
segments.summary: She would rather record with a rhythm section; early on she felt held back by record people who kept her in a style.

segments.chapter: Records of the late 1960s and 70s
segments.title: Big bands and strings versus small groups behind a singer
segments.summary: She prefers a small group to a big orchestra with woodwinds and strings, and talks about how a small group adapts under a singer.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: End of day, the book 'More Than Mere Survival'
segments.summary: Hughes thanks her for a marathon session and she names a 1980 book that profiles her; he calls her a community activist.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: What jazz means, and swing versus jazz
segments.summary: She discusses being called a jazz singer, that swing replaced jazz, ragtime versus jazz, and the 'jazz' label Duke Ellington disliked.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Art Tatum, soloists and small-group playing
segments.summary: They discuss Tatum, spontaneity, and whether she'd sing with a pianist like him, recalling a Boston bill with him.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Working with strings and a harp behind her
segments.summary: She says she can do without strings, compares with the Ellis Larkin trio and early harpists who swung.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Pianists she works with nowadays
segments.summary: She names Dill Jones, Marty Napoleon and the musicians who know where to fit behind her.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: End of session two and introduction to session three with Chester Campbell
segments.summary: Hughes ends session two and explains that Mr. Campbell joined session three for a long conversation that was trimmed.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Chester Campbell's father, a tuba player in Harlem bands
segments.summary: Campbell describes his father, who played E-flat tuba, came to New York in 1926, and gigged with Harlem bandleaders.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Recordings with Cliff Jackson and Cliff as a stride pianist
segments.summary: Campbell mentions a prized 1930 record with Cliff Jackson and other stride piano recordings.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's piano roll and his child prodigy flyer
segments.summary: She took Cliff's piano roll of 'Hock Shop Blues' to the Hall of Fame, and has a 1909 flyer from when he was a boy pianist.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Organists and organ trios
segments.summary: Talk about Richard 'Groove' Holmes and whether she would sing with an organ trio.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Recalling John Kirby's band line-up
segments.summary: Campbell recites the Kirby sextet's personnel and handles a Columbia record of 'Loch Lomond'.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Assembling tapes and a dinner invitation
segments.summary: Hughes explains the tapes assembled from Rutgers and Maxine's 78s; Campbell invites them to dinner.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's 1926 record and the oldest records they have
segments.summary: Cliff's 1926 piano roll and 78 of 'The Entertainer'; the oldest recording of Maxine is on the tape.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: How she began singing and being a rebel in school
segments.summary: She wasn't in a church choir, sang popular songs such as 'I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles' in the Homestead library.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Photographs and the 'Anthology of Jazz' with Cliff's band
segments.summary: They look at a photo and discuss the Columbia anthology that includes Cliff's band, put together by Frank Driggs.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: McKinney's Cotton Pickers and Harlem bandleaders
segments.summary: Campbell remembers tuba and bass players, Don Redman and Harlem big bands.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's influence and Yiddish-speaking musicians
segments.summary: Dizzy's remark about Louis on trumpet and a story of Willie the Lion Smith speaking Yiddish.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Looking at photographs of musicians
segments.summary: They view recent photographs including a Fairfield, Connecticut picture with Erskine Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Travelling abroad with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: She went to Europe nearly every year with the band; her earlier trips were Britain in 1948 and 1953-54.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: The Bob Wilber album and George Duvivier
segments.summary: Campbell praises Wilber and the 1969 album with Gus Johnson and Duvivier, whose Bass Fiddle bar he recalls.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Stockholm photographs and a Johnny Blowers letter
segments.summary: Photos taken in Stockholm and a letter from Johnny Blowers about her work with the Giants of Jazz.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Her Rutgers workshop diploma and the Tony nomination
segments.summary: A 1960 community leadership workshop certificate and a Tony nomination for 'My Old Friends'; she's working harder now.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: The Apollo program and Campbell's record collection
segments.summary: They recall a program about the Apollo Theater and Campbell's priceless albums.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Bronx and Harlem clubs, Irene Reid, Pearl Bailey
segments.summary: Campbell reminisces about Brook Benton, Irene Reid, Lou Donaldson and Pearl Bailey at the Blue Morocco.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Bronx bars and clubs: Jabbo's and the Band Box
segments.summary: Campbell and Maxine place bars near Prospect Avenue and Boston Road where they sang or heard music.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Red Allen's funeral and why the Prospect Avenue neighbors loved him
segments.summary: Stories of Red Allen's death, wreath shaped like a trumpet, and his kindness in the neighborhood; Maxine lived across the street.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Record collections and Ed Beach's WRVR collection
segments.summary: They compare record collections and recall the disk jockey Ed Beach's records and money troubles.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Red Allen with Louis Russell's band and the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Maxine recalls being at the Cotton Club with Louis Russell's band.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Campbell's father's anecdotes about musicians
segments.summary: A funny story about a saxophone player told to Campbell by his father.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Social chatter, a festival of her records and phone numbers
segments.summary: Campbell and Hughes exchange pleasantries, planning a festival of her records.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Al Cooper and a beauty-contest anecdote
segments.summary: Campbell tells about Al Cooper's granddaughter.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Melba Liston, Dizzy's band and valve trombone players
segments.summary: They mention Melba Liston, Ernie Wilkins and Billy Eckstine, whose valve trombone inspired Maxine.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Savoy Sultans, Lionel Hampton and a 1948 Pittsburgh show
segments.summary: Memories of the Savoy Sultans, Rudy Powell and Ralph Cooper's broadcasts.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Jay McShann and women pianists
segments.summary: They recall women pianists such as Mary Lou, Hazel Scott, Beryl Booker, and singer Nellie Lutcher.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Lil Green and the black theater circuit
segments.summary: On the Benny Carter tour: the Lincoln, Howard, Apollo and Royal theaters.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Prospect Avenue and plans to gather local musicians for the House That Jazz Built
segments.summary: She wants Bronx musicians like Skeeter Best and Squash to join the House That Jazz Built, located there since 1975.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Boston Road and Prospect Avenue neighbors: Tyree Glenn, Fats Waller
segments.summary: Campbell recalls where he lived, local businesses, Tyree Glenn, the original Fat Man and Turner's Arcadians.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Campbell's family tree and the idea of writing a book
segments.summary: Campbell's mother made a family tree at 84; Maxine tells him to write a 'Roots'-style book.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Campbell leaves; a 1944 record of Cliff Jackson
segments.summary: Hughes notes Campbell's departure while a 1944 78 plays that Maxine found upstairs in the House That Jazz Built.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's birth and early career
segments.summary: He was born in Washington, D.C., in 1902; she has a flyer and stories he told of early bands.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's musical background and the school of Washington pianists
segments.summary: He studied with teachers; pupils sent a delegate to lessons and passed on what they learned.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cutting contests and friendly rivalry among pianists
segments.summary: Rivalry among stride pianists was friendly, a left-hand style.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: The 1944 Black & White solo piano record
segments.summary: Details of a Cliff solo record made July 15, 1944, and how she announced it at the House.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff's piano roll on 'Parlor Piano' and his 1960s album
segments.summary: The roll appears on albums of piano rolls, and Cliff's Harlem Banjo-era album recalls 'Hockshop Blues'.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff Jackson and Duke Ellington in Washington
segments.summary: They discuss their relationship as young Washington musicians; Cliff did not claim discovering Duke.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff's accompanying work and 52nd Street in 1937
segments.summary: He accompanied early blues singers; on 52nd Street in 1937 he did not remember her.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cafe Society and meeting Cliff again in 1950
segments.summary: Cliff worked at Cafe Society downtown from about 1941; she met him again there in 1950.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff as a character, his clothes and bootlegging; their marriage
segments.summary: A subtly funny man with Stetson hats and Box Back suits; they married in 1950.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff as a solo pianist who disliked accompanying
segments.summary: He wanted recognition as a soloist; he brought friends and Fat Cat into her Town Hall concert.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff's Village years, radio broadcasts and recordings
segments.summary: He played Terrasi's and Gondon's, was broadcast, and made a Harlem Banjo album in the 1950s.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Ed Beach's WRVR radio tribute to Cliff and his archive
segments.summary: Ed Beach dedicated a program to Cliff and played his sideman records; the tapes may go to the Institute.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff's groups at Cafe Society and Wellman Braud
segments.summary: They discuss Village Cats-era recordings and whether Wellman Braud was from Washington.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Edith and Lena Wilson, Adelaide Hall and Black Broadway
segments.summary: Lena is Edith Wilson's sister; Edith was the original Aunt Jemima.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff's work for Joe Davis and the spirituals
segments.summary: During his time with Joe Davis he wrote spirituals sung with a choir.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's eighteen-piece band
segments.summary: From a photograph, Cliff led and arranged for a big band of about eighteen pieces; no recordings known.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Dance bands of the 1920s and Homestead's local bands
segments.summary: They discuss dance bands of the era and the Homestead band her uncle led, and a Whiteman-style concert.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Music around Homestead and Pittsburgh: Lois Deppe and Club Mirrador
segments.summary: Big dances had road bands; local small combos; the Club Mirrador had a nine-piece band led by a woman.

segments.chapter: Jazz, style and Cliff Jackson
segments.title: Pittsburgh Musicians Club and a Roy Eldridge story
segments.summary: On the road she visited the Musicians Club where Roy Eldridge was in town, showing how many good players Pittsburgh had.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: A successful jam night at the House That Jazz Built
segments.summary: On 25 July they held a packed event, with local musicians, and elected Amos president of the musicians' group.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Petty theft at the House and keeping the project going
segments.summary: They sort out a baseball-bat theft case, and she is satisfied with how the neighborhood kids behave.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Footnote on Avis Andrews and Cab Calloway
segments.summary: Hughes adds that photos show Avis Andrews, who sang with Cab Calloway and in the Harold Arlen show 'Great Day'.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Video interviews and plans for the Pittsburgh childhood session
segments.summary: She offers a video interview from January 1979 and the opening of the House in 1975; Hughes steers toward her Pittsburgh years.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Her birth, parents' arrival and paternal grandmother in Homestead
segments.summary: Her father's people came from Coatesville; her paternal grandmother was the first black woman in Homestead.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Grandparents who owned a theater, and where her family came from
segments.summary: A grandmother wound up with property in Coatesville and ran a theater outside Philadelphia.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: How she got the name Marietta
segments.summary: She was named after an aunt, Marietta, and they speculate about the Pennsylvania town.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Her father's siblings, her father the barber and mandolin player
segments.summary: Father's sisters and six brothers; her father was a barber who played mandolin in the family orchestra.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Her father's death and living with Aunt Jo and Paul French
segments.summary: After her father died when she was three she stayed with Aunt Jo, reciting a poem in church.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Her uncle's Homestead band
segments.summary: An integrated brass band with an uncle who played tenor sax and many instruments.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Black population of Homestead and the steel mills
segments.summary: The Black community grew with migration from the South to work in the mills; ethnic mix of Hungarians and Poles; school segregation.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Picnics, grandmother's travels and her mother's second marriage
segments.summary: She visited the valley towns as a youngster; her mother married again and her brother uses the name Williams.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Schools in Homestead and the Ward
segments.summary: She attended the Fourth Ward School and others, lived on a street near the mill; the Hill versus the Ward.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: A tomboy childhood and strict upbringing
segments.summary: She loved athletics and softball and was disciplined by a strict mother.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Religion in the family and Methodist and Baptist churches
segments.summary: Her family wasn't deeply religious, church-hopped between Baptist and Methodist, and she recalls Salvation Army services.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Political consciousness and Black participation in Homestead politics
segments.summary: She became politically active later; Homestead had a Burgess, and few Black people held jobs beyond mill work.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: High school and limited work around Homestead
segments.summary: She finished high school in the late 1920s with little to do afterward in town.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Reading and a piecemeal education
segments.summary: Her education came as she went, through community work, including the East Bronx Community Council.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Music in school: reading music and singing harmony
segments.summary: She learned to read music in school, sang harmony from the school song book, and worked out harmony alone.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Jess, a younger dancer from Homestead
segments.summary: Jess was a couple of years younger and worked as a dancer; she lost touch with him.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Leaving Homestead and how the town has changed
segments.summary: Few people she knew are left; she turned professional in 1936.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Music in the home: the victrola, piano rolls and sheet music
segments.summary: Records and piano rolls such as Fats Waller, song sheets and a victrola in every home.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Listening to blues singers and wanting to sing like Ethel Waters
segments.summary: She listened to classic blues women but wanted to sing like Ethel Waters.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: KDKA radio, the first station
segments.summary: Hughes tells how KDKA started; she listened to music constantly.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Lois Deppe and Wylie Avenue on the Hill
segments.summary: Early memories of Lois Deppe, and going to Wylie Avenue to hear music before turning professional.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Her uncle's Red Hot Peppers band and becoming a regular vocalist
segments.summary: She sang with her uncle's band, becoming regular vocalist around 1934.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Singing with her uncle's group and early performing history
segments.summary: The job lasted a while; she just went along for the ride; she recaps her early appearances and when singing developed.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: The Benjamin Harrison Literary Club
segments.summary: How the downtown club got its name, became a speak-easy after the Volstead Act, and drew mixed crowds after work.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Local bands, Local 471 and Pittsburgh halls, theaters and parks
segments.summary: Swing bands at the Pythian Temple, Syria Mosque, Kennywood Park, and Pittsburgh theaters including burlesque and legitimate houses.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Earl Hines, Don Redman and female orchestra leaders
segments.summary: Hughes asks about local big names; she recalls a woman leader with a five-piece group and the north side.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Pittsburgh clubs and being a girl
segments.summary: She recalls the Leader House and Collins Inn but, as a girl, couldn't go to many clubs.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Occasional singing at parties and the basketball team dances
segments.summary: She sang at parties and after basketball games with a piano in the gym.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: A movie-house contest prize in Rankin
segments.summary: She sang four shows a day for a week, won a prize of under twenty dollars and a taste of show business.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Beginning to try to get work in 1934 with help from uncle Harry
segments.summary: Harry introduced her to musicians and looked for openings, humiliating at first.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Getting the job at the Benjamin Harrison club and the flood
segments.summary: A pianist friend of Harry's heard her; a flood stranded them downtown and Xavier Cugat was in town.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Singing at the tables, tips and the waiter's boost
segments.summary: At the club she sang at tables; another girl was nearly kept instead of her until a waiter intervened; she stayed a year.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Saving money and deciding to look up Gladys Mosier
segments.summary: The club began to draw performers like Gladys Mosier's Ina Ray Hutton band, which led to her New York plan.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: David Obie and Jenny Dillard
segments.summary: David Obie was the waiter who helped; Jenny Dillard came to New York with her and worked at the Onyx Club.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Pittsburgh musicians: Toodle-oo and Boots Swan
segments.summary: She remembers boogie-woogie pianists and Boots Swan, the most popular singer, who never recorded.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Earl Hines, Claude Hopkins and Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: She heard Hines on remote broadcasts and talks about Benny Goodman hiring Fletcher Henderson.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Roy Eldridge, Mary Lou Williams, Litton Garner and Babe Russin
segments.summary: Pittsburgh musicians she knew or didn't, and Babe Russin's presence on her first record.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: 'Trees' and Lois Deppe and Orlando Roberson
segments.summary: Hughes asks about songs she did; Lois Deppe's claim about singing the song first and the idea of the style.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: 'A Night of Stars' benefit and the Courier
segments.summary: A show of artists who came back to Pittsburgh covered by the black newspaper.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: Hemp Pie and other musicians from Pittsburgh and the Midwest
segments.summary: She lists Pittsburgh figures such as George Benson and musicians from Ohio, Detroit and Chicago.

segments.chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
segments.title: End of the fourth session
segments.summary: Hughes thanks her for the trip back and ends the fourth session.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Start of the fifth session and leftover family questions
segments.summary: Hughes opens on 25 September at the House That Jazz Built and begins with grandparents.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Her grandfathers and her maternal grandmother's family
segments.summary: She doesn't remember her grandfathers; her uncle lives in Rankin and the family moved around.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Aunt Mae and Jess Jackson
segments.summary: Aunt Mae's family and when she ran into Jess in 1955.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Her mother, step-father and half brother
segments.summary: Her mother lived until 1959; her stepfather William White; her brother uses the Williams or French name.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: How far she went in school and her extended family
segments.summary: She went to the eleventh grade and finished high school; her mother and family helped with childcare.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The decision to go to New York
segments.summary: Musicians encouraged her; she recaps the Pincus search, auditions and the Onyx Club job.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The management contract with Gladys Mosier and Claude Thornhill
segments.summary: They drew up a contract as personal representatives with 25 percent each; little came of it at first, and Kirby managed himself.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Claude's artistic control, her name change and early publicity
segments.summary: Claude's role was artistic, he picked the name Sullivan, and she tells how Archer Winston's article came about.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The five-year contract, her salary and expenses
segments.summary: She earned about $750 at the club with weekly expenses withheld, and Claude had no business sense.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Claude Thornhill as a person and afterwards
segments.summary: She calls Claude a quiet genius; after their relationship ended she didn't see him for years.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Photographs, sudden fame and its strain
segments.summary: A glamorous photo in November 1939; overnight success was hard on her and she didn't always feel like performing.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: 'Jazzing the classics' and vocal folk-song versions
segments.summary: Kirby's instrumental classics followed 'Loch Lomond'; the folk-song swing treatment was simple but caught on.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The Onyx Club year and the sudden fame of 1937-38
segments.summary: She was at the Onyx from July to December, then midtown and the Cotton Club; she overcame hurdles quickly.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: After Hollywood, Thelma Carpenter and returning to the Onyx
segments.summary: She finished the Hollywood engagement, was perhaps replaced at the Onyx by Thelma Carpenter, and returned for a couple of months.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: A Louisville concert and vaudeville dates
segments.summary: A one-off jazz concert in Louisville; she was mostly doing concerts and vaudeville.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The market for female singers after 'Loch Lomond'
segments.summary: Milt Gabler's claim that her success opened a market for female singers like Billie Holiday; she says most singers had been band vocalists.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: John Kirby as bandleader and the arrangers
segments.summary: Kirby's band backed her on records; he handled band business and chose arrangers such as Lou Singer.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The Kirby and Frankie Newton band shuffle at the Onyx
segments.summary: She discusses the 'giant fight' and how the Onyx band changed after she arrived.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Her marriage to John Kirby and his personality
segments.summary: They were married about 1938 to 1941; she describes a big-hearted, generous man whose lack of planning annoyed her.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Kirby's early life and his charm
segments.summary: Liner-note descriptions of Kirby as a charmer; little is known of his youth.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: After the divorce: later Kirby recordings
segments.summary: She didn't see him after their divorce except once around 1945, and comments on later records with tenor sax.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Studio musicians, Lionel Hampton and Chick Webb in the Arnold Shaw book
segments.summary: Hughes cites Arnold Shaw on musicians; Maxine says many studio musicians sat in on 52nd Street.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Vaudeville at Loew's State and a Benny Goodman concert in Boston
segments.summary: She played vaudeville houses repeatedly and was an added attraction with Goodman in Boston, carrying her own arrangements from Columbia.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Her first vaudeville engagements
segments.summary: Her first vaudeville engagements at Loew's State and the variety acts on the bill.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The Cotton Club and Broadway with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: After 'Going Places' she joined the Cotton Club and a Broadway show; she enjoyed working with Louis.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Making the two movies and the five songs she sang
segments.summary: In both films she was just in the movie; the songs in 'St. Louis Blues' included 'Loch Lomond', and she did little else on set.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The Soundies and a short with Benny Carter
segments.summary: She made two Soundies in the Bronx, including one of 'St. Louis Blues', and Meeker's book lists a Benny Carter short.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Ken Murray's Hollywood revue
segments.summary: She appeared in Ken Murray's revue in Hollywood.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The tour with Benny Carter
segments.summary: They covered twenty-three states on one-nighters in six weeks; local families opened their homes to musicians.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: How the Carter tour came about and the Decca switch
segments.summary: She was contacted under her management contract; unsure if it coincided with signing at Decca.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Preferring small groups with minimal arrangements
segments.summary: She felt boxed in singing with big-band arrangements.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: 'Midnight', 'What a Difference a Day Makes' and her Carter repertoire
segments.summary: Discussion of the songs on the Carter sides and a joke about Dinah Washington.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Being identified with one song and keeping the repertoire current
segments.summary: She says she was stuck with 'Loch Lomond' as an attraction but kept her repertoire fresh.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Her voice, range and style over the years
segments.summary: Her range is the same but the voice has changed; her light voice was natural for the arrangements of the time.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Avoiding imitation and singing songs straight
segments.summary: She stayed away from another singer's style and tried to sing straight.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Being a woman in a man's world; publishers and repertoire
segments.summary: She comments on the word 'standards' and how publishers handle new music.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Hearing like a musician and defining a jazz singer
segments.summary: She says since the 1960s she tried to move away from early style and thinks like a musician.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Scat and her first jazz record
segments.summary: She never went into scat; the Bob Wilber album was her first jazz record, in her own view, the earlier albums were balladeer work.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Her vocal approach from 1937 on and swing as her era
segments.summary: She felt she had the same style but with more freedom; she belongs to the swing era.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Who counts as a jazz singer
segments.summary: They run through Billie Holiday, Ethel Waters, Carmen McRae, Sarah Vaughan, Anita O'Day and Betty Carter and the swing versus modern distinction.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Staying within the melody and improvisation
segments.summary: She likes to stay close to melody; a good song needs no improvisation.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Dinah Shore and Peggy Lee as listeners of her style
segments.summary: Dinah Shore acknowledged her as a major influence; Peggy Lee also mentioned her; she was influenced by Ella, Billie and Ethel Waters.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Mildred Bailey's warning and Midge Williams
segments.summary: Mildred Bailey advised her on style so she wouldn't be a second Ella; Midge Williams was more commercial.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: A newspaper claim about quitting to marry, 1942
segments.summary: An Institute clipping said she'd retire; she married a doctor in 1942 during Le Ruban Bleu.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: The wartime slump in recording and swing 'nipped'
segments.summary: Poor material and the recording ban; Maxine says swing was nipped during the war.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Local talent unappreciated at home and her in-and-out career
segments.summary: Pittsburgh musicians went unrecognized; she's been lucky in dropping in and out, and young people discover swing.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Being 'stuck in a time warp' and today's pop
segments.summary: She doesn't know currently popular tunes; Hughes notes contemporary singers using older repertoire.

segments.chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
segments.title: Younger jazz singers, fusion singers and changing times
segments.summary: They discuss Shirley Horn, Betty Carter, Irene Kral and fusion singers like Urszula Dudziak; she says each has their own era.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: End of session five and start of session six
segments.summary: Hughes closes the fifth session and opens the sixth at Maxine's home on 16 October.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Who guided her career after Claude: Lou Singer, Columbia and MCA
segments.summary: After the break with Claude, Lou Singer arranged for her; Columbia's artists bureau ended and she moved to MCA.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Arrangements on tour, and why she couldn't record 'Trees'
segments.summary: She took about five arrangements on tour; a publisher issue kept her from singing 'Trees'.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Settling into Le Ruban Bleu and living in Harlem
segments.summary: Joined in 1942 after the Carter tour; the club was on East 56th Street; she lived on Conklin Avenue and her money was in escrow.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Illness, her daughter's birth and the Village Vanguard anniversary
segments.summary: She was ill after returning, her daughter was born in 1945, and she thought about stopping as styles changed.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: How Le Ruban Bleu ran: acts, Chittison and the house trio
segments.summary: The club's schedule of acts, Herman Chittison's group with Dave Barber and Sedric Wallace, and why she stayed six years.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Auditions, novelty acts and the supper-club food
segments.summary: No food; the club drew show people; other acts were comedians and novelty; she chose her own material.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Herman Chittison's career and travels
segments.summary: Chittison left the U.S. in the late 1920s and travelled in Europe and India, working for Jacoby; he settled in Ohio.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The Three Deuces with Fats Waller and her accompanists
segments.summary: She sang at the Three Deuces with Fats Waller accompanying her and gets comic songs from working with Fats.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The Village Vanguard: the Three Flames, folk acts and bop
segments.summary: She worked there with groups, folk-oriented bills including Leadbelly, Pete Seeger, the Weavers and Judy Holliday.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Repertoire pressure at the Vanguard and her total four years
segments.summary: She mixed standards with her hit songs and ran into audiences from different countries; she worked there off and on until 1956.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Free-lancing and deciding it was time to stop
segments.summary: Probably theater engagements and Canadian clubs; as a commercial act she couldn't draw, so she retired.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Expected to sing 'Loch Lomond' and a disc jockey's help
segments.summary: She was expected to do her hits and a Washington disc jockey played her records.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Poor distribution of the Andy Razaf album and the label owner
segments.summary: About two hundred albums were pressed and nothing came of it; she likes 'Mound Bayou' and 'Massachusetts'.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Tape end and Hughes's footnotes
segments.summary: Hughes adds footnotes, including one on Fats Waller's death.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Lead sheets, repertoire and the burden of 'Loch Lomond'
segments.summary: She writes lead sheets for her accompanists, fields 'why did you sing Loch Lomond', and says the song has gotten her out of bad situations.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Her two trips to Britain and Ireland
segments.summary: She played the London Casino in 1948 and a variety circuit in 1953-54, transposing arrangements for pit bands.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Declining work, British tour and refusing travel to stay with her daughter
segments.summary: The tour was an exception to fewer bookings; after stopping in '57 she didn't accept offers.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Last appearances before retirement and the South Bay festival
segments.summary: She stopped in 1957 but did the South Bay Jazz Festival in July 1958; Cliff encouraged her.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Practicing trombone and losing the trumpet
segments.summary: She practiced valve trombone, and recently lost her pocket trumpet from a car while on a gig.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The 1958 Seven Ages of Jazz and travelling with Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Her occasional appearances in 1958; Billie Holiday sat beside her on the small plane and seemed bitter.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Clubs around Boston Road and George Duvivier
segments.summary: She recalls Harlem and Bronx clubs before moving and mentions Duvivier.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Rhythm and blues and the crisis in popular music before her retirement
segments.summary: Back from Britain she found the singers doing rhythm and blues; she felt there was no place for her style.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Nostalgia radio and the new swing audience
segments.summary: They discuss WNEW, WEVD, Phil Schaap and how old songs sound new to younger listeners.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Entertainment versus pure jazz and singing the lyric
segments.summary: She sees herself as an entertainer, comparing with instrumentalists who imitate voices, noting Lester Young knowing the words first.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: A rhythm-and-blues arrangement of 'Loch Lomond'
segments.summary: She once recorded an r&b version for a tape that may not have been released.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: An old tape, the outtake album and a film clip of 'Mutiny in the Nursery'
segments.summary: An early-1930s tape is with Alan Eighler; Chertok has the film clip she would like to show.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: W. C. Handy's royalties and the dedication of his cabin
segments.summary: She recounts a Cleveland Press article on Handy's lack of royalties and attending the dedication of his Florence cabin in cold weather.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Her retirement years: daughter's school and community work
segments.summary: Her daughter's school troubles led her to the parents' association, after-school help for children and the Board of Education.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: After-school programs, volunteers and teachers
segments.summary: She describes the programs for children, volunteer parents, and teachers' reactions.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The Opportunity Program and bringing parents into classrooms
segments.summary: She explains how parent involvement became an Opportunity Program, with some teacher resistance.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Invitations to sing again and the Dick Gibson jazz party
segments.summary: She was not ready to stop work and then got invitations that led back to performing with a good reception.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: How the Hoagy Carmichael album came about at the Riverboat
segments.summary: Bob Wilber and Bill Borden, who had known Claude Thornhill, heard her at the Riverboat and used her on the album.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Details of the 1967 Town Hall concert
segments.summary: Town Hall contacted her; the concert used a Dixieland combination without bass.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The Manassas festival recordings and Fat Cat
segments.summary: She sang there because Cliff was going; she was angry about unknowing recording; various Fat Cat albums and liner mix-ups.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: George Buck, Jazzology and the albums in the works
segments.summary: She ran into Buck, producer of Fat Cat's early albums, and has made two more for release, including a Spencer Clark session.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Informal sessions and the quartet format with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: She likes the freer sessions; with the band she sings with a quartet that takes turns filling in like a jam session.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: How her recordings differ from her actual work
segments.summary: She is mainly called for weekend gigs and one-nighters; recording history doesn't reflect her work.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: 'My Old Friends': from La MaMa to Broadway
segments.summary: She got involved through Phil Rose; the show opened Off-Off-Broadway in 1978 and moved to a midtown theater, running April to May.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Trying to record songs from the show
segments.summary: Many viewers wanted a record; she sang 'Thank the Good Lord I'm Not Old' and a label agreed to record two songs.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Acting versus singing, showmanship and projection without a microphone
segments.summary: The techniques differ; theater work needs projection and playing with the audience, and the show was a musical comedy.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The PBS show 'G.I. Jive' and television talk shows
segments.summary: She sang 'Loch Lomond' with a full orchestra at Roseland for Public Television and made talk-show appearances.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Talk shows and advice on surviving in the South Bronx
segments.summary: On TV she sang 'There's Still a Little Starch Left in the Old Girl' and told people to get involved.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Living in the same house and plans for the House That Jazz Built
segments.summary: She has lived in the neighborhood thirty-five years and plans to involve the kids in the House's activities.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Ethel Waters records found at the House and the House's origin
segments.summary: Records found there; the House was a little building bought in memory of Cliff Jackson, with a dorm and visiting musicians such as Vic Dickenson.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: The youth program, kids after school and a deadline of June 1981
segments.summary: After school from three to five kids need supervision; the House aims to give them a proving ground for performance.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Her essential interest and giving kids a chance to perform
segments.summary: Her community work is now primary; singing is second nature; there are no more amateur nights.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Her singing schedule over the next few years
segments.summary: She keeps taking calls but a three-day program limits work; Atlantic City was the last until June 1981.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Upcoming fundraiser at NYU Law School and the membership of the House
segments.summary: The House has about 150 members; young performers and board members like Alan Hanlon will perform.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Running the school program and class sizes
segments.summary: Hughes admires her taking on the school program in a community school.

segments.chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
segments.title: Close of the sixth and final session
segments.summary: Hughes thanks Maxine Sullivan and ends the interview.
